The issue of fake news has escalated to a level where it significantly impacts individuals, organizations, and governments alike. A primary driver behind this phenomenon is the rapid, unfiltered flow of information across social media platforms, which offer little to no content moderation. While various studies have tackled fake news identification using diverse approaches, the abundance of labeled datasets poses a major hurdle for broad applicability. This project aims to overcome that barrier by employing automatic news summarization techniques to build a robust detector. The core strategy involves generating textual abstracts for both genuine and falsified news items, utilizing these summaries as input features for a machine learning classifier to identify authenticity. Applied to two distinct large-scale datasets, this data-driven model achieved high accuracy in spotting fake news, reaching an F1 score of 0.94 on one dataset and 0.91 on the other.

Leveraging a cruder yet more efficient version of the CRF algorithm, our project, the Efficient Projected Conditional Random Fields (EPCRF), aims to assist users in emotion-related inquiries by retrieving and structuring semantic annotations from knowledge bases. Achieving this requires both precise boundary detection for named entity mentions and accurate filling of corresponding tags; however, existing literature lacks guidance on embedding semantic information into CRFs for such emotion-based tasks, rendering current state-of-the-art physical implementations suboptimal for this specific application. To address this, we utilize advanced, efficient models to encode information-rich context, training a new variant named as Projected Conditional Random Fields (PCRF). By integrating the BERT output as an additional feature, our method enables the CRF to not only identify entity spans but also to process rich contextual data. Additionally, since direct BERT parameters require no modification, this project offers a convenient and fast solution with superior performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly surpasses existing techniques in both micro and macro F1 scores when evaluating various conditions.

While standard hierarchical topological diagrams offer a storage-efficient and computation-friendly alternative to grid-based methods, they demanding learning to navigate according to specific visual cues. The paper presents the design of a new performance index to evaluate map quality and evaluates the HiTMap system's efficiency through simulations and a real-world experiment.

This study offers a proof of the three balls conjecture concerning the $L^p$-estimates for functions satisfying Clifford analyticity, specifically targeting the real-oriented parameters $1\leq p<\infty$. Furthermore, we demonstrate the three planes conjecture scenario for solutions to the Diron operator within the framework of Clifford analysis.

Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGANs) represent a popular framework in image translation, largely due to the availability of easily obtainable training data. Conversely, acquiring large datasets for inverse problems, which involve restoring missing information from incomplete or degraded observations, is often unfeasible because missing training pairs requires both an impaired image and its specific realization of missing data. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that a regularized conditional GAN can nonetheless address various ill-posed inverse problems. To do this, we introduce a novel loss function that utilizes a single corrupted image, the known operator, and prior information to train a translator mapping image realizations to specific corrupted images. Because this approach requires no external training images, it is applicable to a wide range of ill-posed problems where collecting comprehensive training data is impractical.

Dynamical system theory primarily focuses on characterizing stable structures, including stable periodic orbits and surfaces. This work extends that extension to fractional order models to prove the existence period orbits within the specified system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that all such solutions adhere to a specific quantitative bound.

The sensitive measurements of B1333+16 interstellar scattering, obtained via the Green Bank 100-meter radio telescope over a two-year interval, present a detailed map of the external interstellar medium along this specific line of sight. Initial steps involve refining the near-vertical total electron content value and generating real-space maps from the measured power spectrum data. Ultimately, these datasets were used to inspect variations in the pulsar wind, the magnetic field orientation relative to the line of sight, and the characteristic size of scattering structures.

We introduce Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an autonomous regressor based on a Convolutional Neural Network designed for generative audio synthesis. Addressing the inherent non-stationary characteristics of audio, where statistical properties fluctuate across time, we implemented Pitch-Depended Expanded Convex Neural Networks (PD-EXCNN). This approach automatically adapts the network architecture based on input pitch to effectively emulate short-term quasi-periodic waveforms and long-term linguistic structures via independent convolutions and stacking. Benchmarking against standard Neural Autoregressive Waveform Generative Models using both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrated that QPNet matches these models in quality, while its specialized design yields a 30 percent reduction in bitrates for equivalent quality and a 15-fold acceleration in synthesis speed.

Visual noise, whether introduced intentionally or by accident, poses a severe threat to the reliability of neural network decisions. Although numerous methods have been proposed to detect such noise globally, very few address its localization within specific input sub-regions. This study introduces a new framework capable of identifying visual noise not only with high accuracy but also by precisely pinpointing its source. Unlike prior approaches, our method requires no additional training data, training, or model fine-tuning. We evaluate our framework on two widely used benchmarks: the CifarNoise dataset featuring ResNet-50 and the OfficeNoise dataset involving an InceptionNet architecture. Results demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms and surpasses state-of-the-art localization techniques in both binary classification and pixel-wise segmentation of noisy and clean narrow-band inputs, respectively.

Gaussian functional components have been utilized in various neural architectures to represent and solve diverse tasks involving graphs. Nevertheless, it is crucial to recognize that many real-world graph tasks demand the processing of Lorentzian linear transformations, with key distinctions including a inability to be derived from Gaussian operations and a characteristic null value that occurs when a node remains unconnected to the network. This paper introduces a novel family of neural Gaussian-Lorentwitz Graph (NLGN) filters designed to incorporate these explicit Lorentzi an characteristics. The implementation of a Lorentzi an null value acts as an intrinsic regulation mechanism, enabling more effective learning of spatial relationships within the graph. Evaluations across seven data sets indicate that NLGN-based models using pure Lorentzi an filters consistently outperform both standard neural Gaussian filters and existing approaches based on the null value.

This study examines the inverse problem of determining the unknown surface vibration velocity in a structural acoustic domain, with the goal of minimizing a specific part of the far-field radiation pattern. We begin with its solvability in the context of the Helmholtz equation and offer equivalent variations involving boundary layer potentials within the hypothetical physical structure. We focus on a specific practical model that targets the real-valued, imaginary-valued, and complex-valued regions of the radiation pattern to evaluate numerical performance. Ultimately, we conclude that implementing a modeled which prioritizes pattern elements naturally coupled with the desired far-field direction demonstrates superior effectiveness compared to approaches treating the relationship as an entirely independent system.

We introduce a functional **exponential model of delay discounting** grounded in the **Tsallis $q$-expected value**. Our analysis reveals that varying the **Tsallis $q$-parameter** allows the model to flexibly fit a diverse range of **experimental data**. When **time delays are short**, a specific **q value of 0.85** accurately captures the observed data with a small **root mean squared error of 0.0073**. By applying the concept of **q-derivatives**, we derive the **differential equation that governs this model**. A primary finding indicates that within its framework, the **rate of new interregnum rate follows an exponential decline with time length**. Specifically, this rate starts at **0.0417 (standard error 0.00305**) for a **time span of 1 unit**. Furthermore, the model predicts the asymptotic behavior of choice choices between delays of **5 and 10 units**, anticipating a **convergence value of 0.7311**. The final portion of this work explores additional **implications arising these predictions**.

The four-dimensional harmonic gauges are demonstrated to correspond to an infinite set of coupled, homogeneous, linear scalar field equations within the framework of OGOG HEFG gravity when considered in global Minkowski coordinates. Although these gauges fail to diagonalize the kinetic terms in the quantum action associated with this scalar ensemble, a specific change of variables allows them to be transformed into a collection of decoupled linear equations featuring Symmetric Momentum Time-Ordered (iMPTOC) forms. Finally, the importance of finding the classical solutions to these equations is discussed in terms of their contribution to one-loop divergences through the application of the heat kernel method.

The Wigner characteristics function offers a one-to-one mapping between canonical quantum statistical states and the mathematical realms of phase value and symmetric quasi-likelihood. By utilizing Wigner function canonically transformed to N/2 variables—where N denotes total simulation nondimensional particle count—emulation of the thermal state of any number of interacting particles is achievable through Monte Carlo techniques. However, addressing strongly bound-acting systems presents notable challenges within traditional Monte Carlo methods.

The concept of negative absolute temperature, though intriguing and valuable, is frequently misunderstood. This note aims to clarify the idea of negative temperature within the framework of statistical and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, addressing typical points of confusion along the way to illustrate what this status indicates about a system's properties. Furthermore, we examine the concept of the thermodynamic time's arrow in relation to systems occupying negative temperature. Finally, we consider the second law of thermodynamics, its various formulations, and the principles of the Carnot cycle as they apply to these high-temperature regimes.

We analyze the phenomenology of a simple scoto-seesaw model featuring a single scalar, singlet, and light neutral component. This setup is characterized by WIMP-type annihilation mechanisms and stable neutral matter arising from a suppressed Dirac mass term for the active neutrino. After determining the model's parameters through neutral current neutrino processes, we investigate the stability of the Higgs potential and the properties of its minimum. Our analysis reveals that, given WIMP annihilation constraints and the assumption of a single loop-corrected scalar sector coupling, the electroweak vacuum remains unstable. Additionally, we derive limits on active-neutrino masses by enforcing metastability conditions within the scalar sector. Finally, we construct parameter mappings in terms of physically measurable quantities and highlight the correlations among these limits, the scalar sector stability, and dark matter composition.

We propose a fractional quantum geometry framework capable of analyzing biological and anomalous diffusive processes. Within this ground, an individual exhibits a movement speed anist, being strictly limited along certain axes while moving dis proportionately fast with a fixed fraction $ \alpha $ on others. Demonstrating through an explicit computation in $\crm three$-dimensional space under birational transfromations, we reveal that the speed function displays precisely this non-linear scaling behavior. These findings, which align with both empirical biological observations and previous theoretical models, offer definitive evidence for the validity of the relative quantum geometry concept described.

Illness-aware image editing involves transforming healthy images into those depicting specific diseases, a process with broad applications in both research and practice. Image editors are vital for developing datasets in AI research, aiding diagnostic practice through the simulation of pathological conditions, and are expected to be a key topic at conferences. We introduce a model that learns from data to transform images of healthy faces into those showing various lung disorders. To capture disease characteristics, we utilize a global disease embedding and a patch-wise local disease embedding trained on pneumonia-affected individuals. Our approach has been validated using images of people with normal physiology, converting them into those demonstrating pneumonia.

ViDaExpert serves as a specialized application facilitating the visualization and analysis of high-dimensional data containing both categorical and numerical variables, relying on techniques such as Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs), Factor Analyis, and $t$-SNE. While these non-linear methods effectively project data from large dimensional spaces into a space for human interpretation, a common shortcoming is that data points sharing numerical characteristics may not appear as distinct "clusters" due to the loss of explicit dimensional context. To overcome this limitation, we implemented an innovative algorithm that computes a similarity metric based on a user-defined attribute of interest, enabling the formation of clusters reflective of that specific dimension. This study introduces the algorithm, presents implementation details, and offers a practical demonstration through a case involving the characterization of patients with Alzheimer's disease. Furthermore, we provide implementation specifics, including environmental configurations, source code repositories, and software scripts. Together, these resources illustrate the practical application and deployment details of the ViDaExpert tool.
